presentingComplaint: Progressive headache, morning vomiting and new right-sided weakness on post-operative day 5, culminating in a witnessed seizure on the surgical ward.
history: 71-year-old woman admitted 5 days earlier for elective right total knee replacement, now on the orthopaedic ward. Background of hypertension, type 2 diabetes and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. Polypharmacy: apixaban (resumed post-op), amlodipine, ramipril, metformin, atorvastatin, plus ward prescriptions of oxycodone PRN, ondansetron and enoxaparin bridging - the team initially attributed her symptoms to opioid effect and post-operative delirium. Over the preceding 3 weeks (before admission) she had a gradually worsening dull frontal headache, worse on waking and on coughing/straining, with two episodes of unexplained morning vomiting she had not reported. Family note she has become uncharacteristically apathetic and forgetful over the last month, with one unwitnessed fall. Reports about 4 kg unintentional weight loss over 2 months. On post-op day 5 she developed clumsiness of the left hand progressing to left arm weakness, then a generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting ~90 seconds with post-ictal confusion. No fever, neck stiffness or photophobia. Ex-smoker (30 pack-years).
examination: Drowsy but rousable, GCS 14 (E3 V5 M6) post-ictally, improving. Fundoscopy shows bilateral papilloedema. Left upper and lower limb pyramidal weakness (MRC 4/5) with a left pronator drift and extensor left plantar; mild left facial asymmetry. No neck stiffness, Kernig negative. Apathetic affect with impaired attention and short-term recall on cognitive screen. Surgical knee wound clean and dry. No rash. Chest clear, heart sounds normal with an irregularly irregular pulse.

labs.note: Mild hyponatraemia (SIADH-pattern), otherwise unremarkable; infective/metabolic screen negative

imaging: CT head (non-contrast, urgent post-seizure): right frontoparietal ill-defined hypodensity with surrounding vasogenic oedema, effacement of adjacent sulci and 6 mm midline shift; no acute haemorrhage, no extra-axial collection, no established infarct. MRI brain with contrast: solitary ~3.5 cm intra-axial right frontal mass with irregular heterogeneous rim enhancement, central necrosis and extensive surrounding T2/FLAIR vasogenic oedema; features consistent with a high-grade glioma or solitary metastasis. MR spectroscopy shows raised choline:NAA. Staging CT chest/abdomen/pelvis arranged to exclude a primary.
microbiology: Not indicated; no clinical features of CNS infection. Blood cultures (sent to exclude sepsis as a cause of post-op deterioration) negative. Lumbar puncture contraindicated due to mass effect and midline shift.
differentialDiagnoses: Primary brain tumour (high-grade glioma) vs solitary cerebral metastasis
Chronic subdural haematoma (elderly, anticoagulated, prior fall)
finalDiagnosis: Solitary intra-axial brain mass lesion (high-grade glioma vs metastasis) presenting with raised intracranial pressure, focal deficit and seizure - unmasked during a post-operative hospital admission and initially mistaken for opioid effect/delirium.
citations: NICE - Brain tumours (primary) and brain metastases in adults, NG99, 2018
EANO - Guidelines on diagnosis and treatment of adult diffuse gliomas, 2021
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Primary and Metastatic Tumors of the Nervous System
stewardship: Not applicable - non-infective mass lesion. No antimicrobials indicated; avoid reflex empirical antibiotics for post-operative deterioration once CNS infection is excluded. Focus is dexamethasone for symptomatic peri-tumoural oedema, seizure management, and urgent neurosurgical/neuro-oncology referral for tissue diagnosis.
contraindications: Lumbar puncture contraindicated - mass effect with 6 mm midline shift (risk of herniation)
Withhold apixaban / anticoagulation pending exclusion of intracranial haemorrhage and neurosurgical planning; balance against AF stroke risk
Avoid further sedating opioids that mask conscious-level deterioration; review polypharmacy
Correct hyponatraemia slowly to avoid osmotic demyelination
edgeCases: Post-operative delirium and opioid analgesia masked progressive focal signs - anchoring bias delayed neuroimaging
Anticoagulation and a prior fall make chronic subdural haematoma the key mimic to exclude on imaging
Solitary ring-enhancing lesion also raises abscess/tuberculoma; clinical context (afebrile, no infective markers) and MRS favour neoplasm
Mild hyponatraemia may reflect tumour-associated SIADH rather than a primary metabolic cause
expectedMaiK: Recognise new focal neurology + seizure + raised-ICP features in a hospitalised elderly patient as a structural intracranial lesion (not delirium/opioid effect), obtain urgent contrast MRI, start dexamethasone for symptomatic oedema, manage the seizure, hold anticoagulation, and refer to neurosurgery/neuro-oncology for tissue diagnosis and staging.
expectedNextQuestions: Character and timing of the headache (worse on waking, coughing/straining)?
Any preceding subacute cognitive/personality change or weight loss?
History of fall or head injury while on anticoagulation?
Smoking history or known primary malignancy (metastasis risk)?
Current opioid/sedative doses and other CNS-active medications?
expectedInvestigations: Urgent non-contrast CT head, then MRI brain with contrast
CT chest/abdomen/pelvis to identify a primary if metastasis suspected
Serum sodium/osmolality and paired urine for SIADH
Coagulation profile and review of anticoagulation
Neurosurgical referral for biopsy/resection and histology
regressionAssertions: Top diagnosis must be brain_tumour (solitary intra-axial mass with rim enhancement and vasogenic oedema)
Must recommend contrast MRI brain and neurosurgical referral for tissue diagnosis
Must NOT recommend antibiotics or antivirals (non-infective)
Must flag lumbar puncture as contraindicated due to mass effect/midline shift
Must recommend dexamethasone for symptomatic peri-tumoural oedema and holding anticoagulation
